title: Correlation
body:
[[Linear Regression]] fits a line. Correlation asks how well the line describes the data, and gives
one unit-free number for it.

## Covariance first

$$
\text{Cov}(X,Y) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})
$$

Which is exactly the [[Variance]] formula with one of the two deviation factors swapped for the
other variable, so **variance is a variable's covariance with itself**. It is positive when the two
tend to be above their means together, negative when one is up while the other is down.

Its problem is units. Covariance of height and weight is in centimetre-kilograms, and its size
depends on the scales, so a covariance of 200 means nothing on its own.

## Pearson's $r$

Dividing by both standard deviations removes the units:

$$
r = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{s_x s_y}
$$

$$
-1 \leq r \leq 1
$$

$r = \pm 1$ is a perfect line, $r = 0$ is no *linear* association. Sign is the direction of the
slope, magnitude is how tightly the points cluster around it. Because it is standardised, $r$ is
unchanged by rescaling either variable, which is what makes it comparable across studies.

Geometrically $r$ is the cosine of the angle between the two centred data vectors, which is the
[[Inner Product]] and [[Projection]] view in MATH 2303. **Uncorrelated means orthogonal**, and that
is why [[Principal Component Analysis|PCA]]'s components come out uncorrelated: they are orthogonal
eigenvectors of the covariance matrix built from exactly these numbers.

## $r^2$

The **coefficient of determination**: the proportion of the variance in $y$ that the regression line
accounts for.

$$
r^2 = \frac{\text{SS}_{\text{explained}}}{\text{SS}_{\text{total}}}
= 1 - \frac{\text{SSR}}{\text{SS}_{\text{total}}}
$$

$r^2 = 0.64$ means the line explains 64% of the variation and 36% is left in the residuals. It is
the same explained-over-total ratio [[ANOVA]] computes, and the same Pythagorean split
[[Least Squares]] describes: total squared length equals explained plus residual, because the two
components are perpendicular.

$r^2$ is more honest to report than $r$, since $r = 0.7$ sounds like most of the story and explains
under half of it.

## What $r$ misses

> [!warning] Correlation is not causation, and that is not its only limitation
> - **Not causation.** $X$ may cause $Y$, $Y$ may cause $X$, a third variable may cause both, or it
>   may be coincidence. Only a controlled experiment separates those, and observational data never
>   does no matter how large.
> - **Linear only.** A perfect parabola symmetric about the origin has $r = 0$. Zero correlation
>   means no *linear* association, never independence, which is the [[Random Variable]] point that
>   $E[XY] = E[X]E[Y]$ does not imply independence.
> - **Outlier sensitive.** One point can create a strong $r$ out of a formless cloud, or destroy a
>   real one. Anscombe's quartet is four datasets with identical $r$, means, and regression lines
>   and completely different scatter plots.
> - **Aggregation changes it.** Pooling groups can reverse a correlation present in every group
>   (Simpson's paradox), which is [[Conditional Probability]]'s conditional-independence problem
>   showing up in continuous data.
>
> The fix for all four is the same: **plot it.** See [[Descriptive Statistics]].

## Related

- [[Linear Regression]]: $\beta_1 = r(s_y/s_x)$, so the two are computed from the same sums
- [[Variance]]: covariance is that formula with two variables
- [[ANOVA]]: the same explained-versus-total decomposition
- [[Principal Component Analysis]] and [[Inner Product]] (MATH 2303): $r$ as a cosine, and the
  covariance matrix as the object PCA eigen-decomposes
